digestion of amylopectin produces branched oligosaccharides called a-dextrins, as well as maltose and maltotriose (Gray, 2000).
Salivary and pancreatic amylases break down amylose to produce glucose oligosaccharides and disaccharides with a-1,4 glyco-
sidic bonds, and amylopectin to produce glucose oligosaccharides and disaccharides with a-1,4 and a-1,6 glycosidic bonds (Letur-
que and Brot-Laroche, 2013). In both cases, free glucose molecules account for only a small amount (about 4%) of the digestion
products released (Yook and Robyt, 2002).
The brush border of the small intestine contains an ample amount of oligosaccharidases, which consist primarily of
a glucosidases, and catalyze the ﬁnal reactions of starch digestion by cleaving the a-1,4 glycosidic bonds between glucose
molecules one at a time (Semenza and Auricchio, 1991). Alpha glucosidases (i.e., sucrase, a-dextrinase, glucoamylase, and
trehalase) have the ability to break down a-1,4 glycosidic bonds, but they bind with high afﬁnity to the substrate indicated
